The results add evidence to emerging observations about feature manifolds, suggesting that geodesic distances track true distances and manifolds are organized around flat representations with additional curvature.

papers.title: Neural Correlates of Language Models Are Specific to Human Language
papers.research_question: Are correlations between language model hidden states and fMRI brain responses robust to dimensionality concerns, and are they specific to models trained on human language and dependent on positional encoding?
papers.core_contribution: The study confirms that correlations between transformer language model hidden states and human brain activity during language tasks are robust, specific to language-trained models, and heavily dependent on positional encodings.
papers.conclusion: The internal representations of transformer language models are strongly correlated with human brain activity during language processing, and this alignment is specific to language-trained models and relies on positional information.
papers.key_findings:
Removing positional encodings significantly reduces brain-model correlations and distorts the geometric similarity between model and brain representational spaces.
Dimensionality reduction via PCA does not eliminate the correlations, indicating they are not an artifact of the curse of dimensionality.
Models trained on non-linguistic data (protein sequences) show negligible alignment with brain activity, confirming the language-specificity of the effects.
Causal (decoder-only) language models show higher alignment with brain activity than bidirectional models.
The geometric structure of model and brain representations, measured by CKA and Gromov-Wasserstein distance, is similar and degrades when positional information is removed.
papers.limitation:
The dataset includes only 243 stimuli and 6 subjects, limiting statistical power and generalizability.
The head-wise analysis pooled voxels across cortical regions without distinguishing between different regions of interest.
The study uses text-only models and fMRI data from reading tasks; future work should use modality-matched datasets (e.g., audio models with spoken language tasks).
future_direction: Increase the number of subjects and model diversity to improve statistical power and generalizability.
Conduct finer-grained region-of-interest (ROI) by head analysis to reveal differential alignment patterns.
Use modality-matched datasets (e.g., spoken-language tasks with audio models) to disentangle task effects from representational differences.
papers.abstract: Previous work has shown correlations between the hidden states of large language models and fMRI brain responses, on language tasks. These correlations have been taken as evidence of the representational similarity of these models and brain states. This study tests whether these previous results are robust to several possible concerns. Specifically this study shows: (i) that the previous results are still found after dimensionality reduction, and thus are not attributable to the curse of dimensionality; (ii) that previous results are confirmed when using new measures of similarity; (iii) that correlations between brain representations and those from models are specific to models trained on human language; and (iv) that the results are dependent on the presence of positional encoding in the models. These results confirm and strengthen the results of previous research and contribute to the debate on the biological plausibility and interpretability of state-of-the-art large language models.

papers.title: The Representation and Recall of Interwoven Structured Knowledge in LLMs: A Geometric and Layered Analysis
papers.research_question: How do LLMs encode interwoven scientific knowledge, and do they reflect geometric structures like the periodic table?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode scientific knowledge in geometric structures, such as a 3D spiral aligning with the periodic table, representing knowledge as interwoven manifolds rather than isolated facts.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop internal representations that reflect the structured geometry of scientific knowledge, representing symbolic knowledge as geometry-aware, interwoven manifolds.
papers.key_findings:
A 3D spiral structure is observed in hidden states that aligns with the periodic table.
Middle layers encode continuous attributes enabling indirect recall, while deeper layers sharpen categorical distinctions.
Linguistic context increasingly shapes representations in later layers.
Middle layers have strong linear associations between related attributes, which weaken in deeper layers.
papers.limitation:
Prompts are focused on chemical elements and may not extend to domains with more abstract features.
Hypothesis-driven validation may oversimplify LLMs' non-linear interactions.
future_direction: Further investigation into how LLMs represent and reason about scientific knowledge, such as materials property prediction.
Informing the design of downstream embedding-based tasks.
papers.abstract: This study investigates how large language models (LLMs) represent and recall multi-associated attributes across transformer layers. We show that intermediate layers encode factual knowledge by superimposing related attributes in overlapping spaces, along with effective recall even when attributes are not explicitly prompted. In contrast, later layers refine linguistic patterns and progressively separate attribute representations, optimizing task-specific outputs while appropriately narrowing attribute recall. We identify diverse encoding patterns including, for the first time, the observation of 3D spiral structures when exploring information related to the periodic table of elements. Our findings reveal a dynamic transition in attribute representations across layers, contributing to mechanistic interpretability and providing insights for understanding how LLMs handle complex, interrelated knowledge.

papers.title: Jump to Conclusions: Short-Cutting Transformers With Linear Transformations
papers.research_question: Is there a more accurate way to cast hidden representations into final representation substitutes than interpreting them as they are (identity mapping)?
papers.core_contribution: A simple method using linear transformations to cast hidden representations to final-layer substitutes, which improves interpretability and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Linear mappings provide a simple and effective way to enhance the utilization of hidden representations for interpretability and efficiency, revealing linear structure in transformer components.
papers.key_findings:
Linear mappings (mat) consistently outperform identity mapping (id) in approximating future hidden representations and final predictions.
The method allows accurate prediction estimation from early layers, showing that models often predict the final output early.
The learned linear mappings generalize well across different model scales and data distributions.
When applied to early exiting, the method saves additional layers (e.g., 7.9% for GPT-2, 5.4% for BERT) while retaining 95% accuracy.
Attention sub-modules are the most tolerant to linear approximation compared to FFN and layer normalization.
papers.limitation:
Focuses only on linear transformations, leaving affine or non-linear transformations for future work.
Does not elucidate the reason for the linear structure observed in transformer inference.
Only considers post-hoc interpretability (analyzing trained models without changing weights).
Experiments are conducted only on English data.
future_direction: Exploring affine or non-linear transformations for casting hidden representations.
Integrating linear mappings into model training rather than only post-hoc analysis.
Breaking the computation into parallel tasks to improve efficiency.
Comparing the method with other approaches like Belrose et al. (2023).
Investigating the reasons for the linear structure in transformer components.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models create hidden representations of their inputs at every layer, but only use final-layer representations for prediction. This obscures the internal decision-making process of the model and the utility of its intermediate representations. One way to elucidate this is to cast the hidden representations as final representations, bypassing the transformer computation in-between. In this work, we suggest a simple method for such casting, using linear transformations. This approximation far exceeds the prevailing practice of inspecting hidden representations from all layers, in the space of the final layer. Moreover, in the context of language modeling, our method produces more accurate predictions from hidden layers, across various model scales, architectures, and data distributions. This allows "peeking" into intermediate representations, showing that GPT-2 and BERT often predict the final output already in early layers. We then demonstrate the practicality of our method to recent early exit strategies, showing that when aiming, for example, at retention of 95% accuracy, our approach saves additional 7.9% layers for GPT-2 and 5.4% layers for BERT. Last, we extend our method to linearly approximate sub-modules, finding that attention is most tolerant to this change. Our code and learned mappings are publicly available at https://github.com/sashayd/mat.

papers.title: On Hierarchical Encoding and Reasoning in Deep Transformer-based Generative Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internalize hierarchical structures from data, what is the relationship between this internalization and behaviors like generalization versus memorization, and how can insights into hierarchical reasoning guide the development of more unified, robust, and interpretable multimodal systems?
papers.core_contribution: This thesis investigates how Transformer models learn and represent hierarchical structures, develops methods to probe these structures and mitigate harmful memorization, introduces the PSViT model for hierarchical video prediction, and demonstrates a unified next-frame prediction framework for multimodal tasks.
papers.conclusion: The capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.
papers.key_findings:
Bidirectional Transformer models (e.g., BERT) concentrate hierarchical linguistic information near the top layers, while autoregressive/permutation-masked models (e.g., GPT-2, XLNet, Reformer) distribute it more evenly.
Verbatim memorization during fine-tuning is often preceded by a spike in n-gram overlap, which can be used for early-stopping or regularization to reduce leakage by up to 90%.
The PSViT model, designed with hierarchical priors, outperforms latent-space baselines on physical simulation benchmarks, extending accurate prediction horizons by up to 50%.
Abstract physical parameters governing video dynamics are most linearly recoverable from the middle layers of PSViT, mirroring the mid-layer abstraction peak for linguistic hierarchy.
Diverse tasks across text, image, audio, and video can be reformulated into a unified next-frame prediction task, enabling a single PSViT-based model to achieve competitive performance without modality-specific encoders.
papers.limitation:
Probing tasks relied primarily on English datasets (SST, PTB), limiting linguistic diversity.
Memorization experiments used datasets of up to 5,000 samples and greedy decoding; different scales or decoding strategies may alter dynamics.
PSViT was evaluated at 128x128 resolution on deterministic simulations; generalizability to complex real-world video is untested.
The multimodal model was trained separately per task; joint multitask training might better foster shared representations.
future_direction: Extend ancestor probing to morphologically rich languages, different syntactic formalisms, and broader discourse structures.
Scale the n-gram-aware loss regularizer to operate efficiently on hundreds of billions of tokens.
Test PSViT on larger-scale, stochastic, real-world video and integrate differentiable renderers for more direct interpretability.
Explore joint multitask training on a diverse corpus of reformulated multimodal data and richer encodings within the visual canvas.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in generative Transformer-based foundation models have driven remarkable progress in artificial intelligence, yet their internal mechanisms for representing complex hierarchical structures remain largely unknown, posing significant challenges for interpretability, safety, and robust generalisation. This thesis aims to progress on these issues by systematically investigating how such models internalise hierarchical structures, the relationship between this learning and behaviours like generalisation versus memorisation, and how hierarchical principles can inform the development of safer, more accurate, generative models. To this end, we first introduce novel probing techniques to map the layer-wise emergence of linguistic hierarchies in language models and extend this analysis to the visual domain by developing PSViT: a pixel-space Transformer with hierarchical decompositions of video image patches, shown to learn and generalise hierarchical physical dynamics from raw video data. We investigate memorisation during fine-tuning, establishing an n-gram based early warning signal for verbatim leakage and proposing scalable defences that promote structural generalisation over verbatim memorisation. Building on these insights, we further demonstrate that a unified next-frame prediction framework enables a single model to process text, images, audio, and video without modality-specific encoders, thereby learning shared hierarchical patterns across these diverse inputs. Collectively, our findings underscore that the capacity to learn and represent hierarchical structure is a fundamental characteristic of Transformer models, and that a focused analysis of these underpinnings is crucial for advancing more capable, interpretable, and safer artificial intelligence.

papers.title: Transformers as Multi-task Learners: Decoupling Features in Hidden Markov Models
papers.research_question: How do Transformers achieve multi-task generalization? Specifically, what are the layerwise mechanisms by which they represent and process sequential information?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformers learn local features in lower layers and decoupled, temporally disentangled features in upper layers when modeling Hidden Markov Models, and provides theoretical constructions that align with these observations.
papers.conclusion: This work advances theoretical and empirical understanding of how Transformers achieve strong generalization across sequence learning tasks, showing they transition from local feature learning in lower layers to decoupled representations in upper layers, providing a principled explanation for their expressiveness and efficiency in multi-task and in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Well-trained Transformers achieve high accuracy under in-context learning on HMMs, with performance improving as more input-output examples are provided or as sequence length increases.
Lower layers of Transformers focus on learning local representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens.
Upper layers develop decoupled, temporally disentangled representations that are less tied to specific input positions and encode higher-level abstractions.
Transformers gradually recognize task identity across layers, with hidden state identification occurring earlier than task identification, indicating a layerwise processing hierarchy.
The theoretical construction demonstrates that Transformers can approximate low-rank HMMs using a fixed-length memory structure, enabling effective in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Analysis is limited to Hidden Markov Models and may not generalize to more complex settings.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more general assumptions and more complex model settings.
papers.abstract: Transformer based models have shown remarkable capabilities in sequence learning across a wide range of tasks, often performing well on specific task by leveraging input-output examples. Despite their empirical success, a comprehensive theoretical understanding of this phenomenon remains limited. In this work, we investigate the layerwise behavior of Transformers to uncover the mechanisms underlying their multi-task generalization ability. Taking explorations on a typical sequence model, i.e, Hidden Markov Models, which are fundamental to many language tasks, we observe that: first, lower layers of Transformers focus on extracting feature representations, primarily influenced by neighboring tokens; second, on the upper layers, features become decoupled, exhibiting a high degree of time disentanglement. Building on these empirical insights, we provide theoretical analysis for the expressiveness power of Transformers. Our explicit constructions align closely with empirical observations, providing theoretical support for the Transformer's effectiveness and efficiency on sequence learning across diverse tasks.

papers.title: Circuit Compositions: Exploring Modular Structures in Transformer-Based Language Models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the modularity of neural networks by analyzing circuits for compositional subtasks, and whether functionally similar circuits can be composed to represent more complex capabilities.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces activation pruning through continuous sparsification for automatic circuit discovery, analyzes the modularity of circuits for compositional tasks, and shows that circuits can be composed via set operations to represent more complex functions.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates a method for circuit discovery and shows that transformer-based models exhibit modularity, with circuits for related tasks sharing nodes and being composable to handle more complex operations.
papers.key_findings:
Activation pruning through continuous sparsification successfully identifies faithful and minimal circuits for each string-edit subtask.
Functionally similar circuits exhibit significant node overlap and cross-task faithfulness.
Circuits can be combined through set operations (e.g., union) to create subnetworks that perform tasks beyond the original circuits.
The copy circuit is sparse and relies heavily on cross-attention modules, while binary circuits like prepend are larger and more complex.
Circuits identified via mean ablation are more faithful than those via zero ablation, and the ablation paradigm affects the identified nodes.
papers.limitation:
The method does not guarantee completeness of the identified circuits.
The choice of ablation value (mean vs zero) affects the identified circuits, indicating a dependence on the ablation paradigm.
The study is limited to a small model and synthetic dataset, and may not generalize to larger models and more diverse tasks.
future_direction: Incorporate completeness into the optimization framework for circuit discovery.
Scale the approach to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: A fundamental question in interpretability research is to what extent neural networks, particularly language models, implement reusable functions through subnetworks that can be composed to perform more complex tasks. Recent advances in mechanistic interpretability have made progress in identifying $\textit{circuits}$, which represent the minimal computational subgraphs responsible for a model's behavior on specific tasks. However, most studies focus on identifying circuits for individual tasks without investigating how functionally similar circuits $\textit{relate}$ to each other. To address this gap, we study the modularity of neural networks by analyzing circuits for highly compositional subtasks within a transformer-based language model. Specifically, given a probabilistic context-free grammar, we identify and compare circuits responsible for ten modular string-edit operations. Our results indicate that functionally similar circuits exhibit both notable node overlap and cross-task faithfulness. Moreover, we demonstrate that the circuits identified can be reused and combined through set operations to represent more complex functional model capabilities.

papers.title: Characterizing Intrinsic Compositionality in Transformers with Tree Projections
papers.research_question: Does the transformer learn a tree-like computation when trained on language data, and how can we measure its tree-structuredness?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces an unsupervised, parameter-free method to functionally project transformers into tree-structured networks, showing that transformers become more tree-like during training and that tree-structuredness predicts compositional generalization.
papers.conclusion: Overall, our results suggest that making further progress on human-like compositional generalization might require inductive biases that encourage the emergence of latent tree-like structure.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers become more tree-like over training on sequence transduction tasks.
Tree projections sometimes align with gold syntax.
Induced trees reflect contextual dependence structure.
Tree-structuredness correlates better with compositional generalization than in-domain accuracy.
Self-supervised training does not lead to tree-like computation in low data regimes.
papers.abstract: When trained on language data, do transformers learn some arbitrary computation that utilizes the full capacity of the architecture or do they learn a simpler, tree-like computation, hypothesized to underlie compositional meaning systems like human languages? There is an apparent tension between compositional accounts of human language understanding, which are based on a restricted bottom-up computational process, and the enormous success of neural models like transformers, which can route information arbitrarily between different parts of their input. One possibility is that these models, while extremely flexible in principle, in practice learn to interpret language hierarchically, ultimately building sentence representations close to those predictable by a bottom-up, tree-structured model. To evaluate this possibility, we describe an unsupervised and parameter-free method to \emph{functionally project} the behavior of any transformer into the space of tree-structured networks. Given an input sentence, we produce a binary tree that approximates the transformer's representation-building process and a score that captures how "tree-like" the transformer's behavior is on the input. While calculation of this score does not require training any additional models, it provably upper-bounds the fit between a transformer and any tree-structured approximation. Using this method, we show that transformers for three different tasks become more tree-like over the course of training, in some cases unsupervisedly recovering the same trees as supervised parsers. These trees, in turn, are predictive of model behavior, with more tree-like models generalizing better on tests of compositional generalization.

papers.title: Inseq: An Interpretability Toolkit for Sequence Generation Models
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Inseq, a Python library for interpretability analyses of sequence generation models, enabling feature attribution and internal information extraction for popular Transformer architectures.
papers.conclusion: Inseq is a versatile toolkit for interpreting sequence generation models and has the potential to drive progress in explainable language generation by centralizing good practices and enabling reproducible evaluations.
papers.key_findings:
In a gender bias case study using machine translation models, attribution scores for source occupation terms showed significant correlation with gender stereotypes in U.S. labor statistics, and contrastive probability differences effectively uncovered bias.
The proposed Contrastive Attribution Tracing (CAT) method, using layer gradient × activation, efficiently located intermediate layers in GPT-2 important for factual knowledge recall, matching results from more computationally intensive patching-based approaches.
The Inseq toolkit centralizes access to a broad set of feature attribution methods for sequence generation, providing an intuitive and extensible interface for interpretability research.
papers.limitation:
Attribution methods lack clear-cut guarantees in identifying specific model behaviors and are prone to user biases; explanations should not be adopted in high-risk, user-facing contexts.
The toolkit does not provide explicit ways of evaluating the quality of produced attributions in terms of faithfulness or plausibility.
The gender bias case study assumes a simplified binary gender concept, which may not capture the full complexity of gender identity.
future_direction: Continuously expand the library by adding support for a wider range of attribution methods (e.g., Guided Integrated Gradients, LRP, Attention Rollout).
Improve result visualization using an interactive interface backed by Gradio Blocks.
Work on interoperability features with other tools (e.g., ferret) to simplify evaluation of sequence attributions.
papers.abstract: Past work in natural language processing interpretability focused mainly on popular classification tasks while largely overlooking generation settings, partly due to a lack of dedicated tools. In this work, we introduce Inseq, a Python library to democratize access to interpretability analyses of sequence generation models. Inseq enables intuitive and optimized extraction of models' internal information and feature importance scores for popular decoder-only and encoder-decoder Transformers architectures. We showcase its potential by adopting it to highlight gender biases in machine translation models and locate factual knowledge inside GPT-2. Thanks to its extensible interface supporting cutting-edge techniques such as contrastive feature attribution, Inseq can drive future advances in explainable natural language generation, centralizing good practices and enabling fair and reproducible model evaluations.

papers.title: Theoretical Analysis of Positional Encodings in Transformer Models: Impact on Expressiveness and Generalization
papers.research_question: What classes of sequence-to-sequence functions can a transformer approximate under different positional encoding schemes? How do positional encodings affect a transformer's ability to generalize and extrapolate to sequences longer than those seen during training?
papers.core_contribution: Presents a unified theoretical framework for analyzing positional encodings in transformers, deriving expressiveness definitions, generalization bounds, and extrapolation analyses, and proposes novel orthogonal function-based encoding schemes.
papers.conclusion: Positional encodings fundamentally shape a transformer's capabilities. The theoretical framework, combined with novel PE schemes and lightweight validation, lays the groundwork for more robust, generalizable, and extrapolatable transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
All common positional encodings yield universal approximation for fixed-length sequences, with ALiBi extending universality to arbitrary lengths.
Generalization bounds for transformer classes depend on input norm bounds; normalized wavelet and Legendre encodings match sinusoidal PEs.
ALiBi's linear bias ensures graceful extrapolation up to a factor of c*N_max, with error growing linearly in distance beyond training length.
Wavelet-based encodings exhibit exponential decay in encoding differences beyond N_max, ensuring strong extrapolation.
Lightweight experiments on a synthetic running-sum task show wavelet-based encodings outperform other methods when extrapolating to 4x training length.
papers.limitation:
Focuses on transformer encoders without layer normalization, dropout, or multi-head complexities; including these may affect Lipschitz constants and generalization.
Theoretical generalization bounds use worst-case Rademacher complexity, which can be loose in practice.
Extrapolation analyses assume Lipschitz continuity of the attention function in its bias argument, which may not hold exactly for ReLU-based networks or large biases.
Experiments use a minimal transformer on a synthetic task; real-world benchmarks may reveal additional behaviors.
future_direction: Extend expressiveness and generalization analyses to multi-head settings, accounting for head interactions and layer normalization.
Investigate methods to adapt ALiBi's slope dynamically based on sequence length or task.
Explore other orthogonal function families tailored for specific domains (e.g., vision sequences, time-series).
Benchmark wavelet and Legendre encodings on real-world tasks that require long-context reasoning.
Extend the information-theoretic perspective to quantify how much positional mutual information is transferred across layers.
papers.abstract: Positional encodings are a core part of transformer-based models, enabling processing of sequential data without recurrence. This paper presents a theoretical framework to analyze how various positional encoding methods, including sinusoidal, learned, relative, and bias-based methods like Attention with Linear Biases (ALiBi), impact a transformer's expressiveness, generalization ability, and extrapolation to longer sequences. Expressiveness is defined via function approximation, generalization bounds are established using Rademacher complexity, and new encoding methods based on orthogonal functions, such as wavelets and Legendre polynomials, are proposed. The extrapolation capacity of existing and proposed encodings is analyzed, extending ALiBi's biasing approach to a unified theoretical context. Experimental evaluation on synthetic sequence-to-sequence tasks shows that orthogonal transform-based encodings outperform traditional sinusoidal encodings in generalization and extrapolation. This work addresses a critical gap in transformer theory, providing insights for design choices in natural language processing, computer vision, and other transformer applications.

papers.title: Learning interpretable positional encodings in transformers depends on initialization
papers.research_question: How does the initialization of a learnable positional encoding affect its interpretability and generalization performance in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Small-norm initialization of learnable positional encodings enables learning of interpretable positional representations that enhance generalization in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Learning interpretable positional encodings depends on initialization, with small-norm initialization leading to interpretable PEs and enhanced generalization performance.
papers.key_findings:
Learnable PEs initialized with small norms achieve better generalization performance on the LST task compared to large-norm initializations and standard PE schemes.
Learnable PEs with small norms learn attention maps that are more aligned with the ground truth 2D positional encoding.
The learned PE embeddings with small norms approximate the ground truth 2D PE after training.
In a nonlinear network simulation, small-norm initialized PEs recover the underlying network modularity.
In fMRI data, small-norm initialized PEs learn a modular organization that reflects the brain's functional networks and improve prediction performance.
papers.limitation:
It is unclear how well the approach generalizes to tasks with arbitrary number of elements or dynamic changes (length generalization in 2D or higher).
For some tasks like next-token prediction or arithmetic, standard PEs may be more appropriate.
The learned PE is linearly superimposed on tokens, which may limit generalization to more complex tasks; future work could explore nonlinear PE embeddings.
future_direction: Generalizing to tasks with arbitrary number of elements or dynamic changes.
Learning nonlinear PE embeddings as a function of token embeddings.
Better theoretical understanding of how initialization, architecture, and optimizer interact.
papers.abstract: In transformers, the positional encoding (PE) provides essential information that distinguishes the position and order amongst tokens in a sequence. Most prior investigations of PE effects on generalization were tailored to 1D input sequences, such as those presented in natural language, where adjacent tokens (e.g., words) are highly related. In contrast, many real world tasks involve datasets with highly non-trivial positional arrangements, such as datasets organized in multiple spatial dimensions, or datasets for which ground truth positions are not known. Here we find that the choice of initialization of a learnable PE greatly influences its ability to learn interpretable PEs that lead to enhanced generalization. We empirically demonstrate our findings in three experiments: 1) A 2D relational reasoning task; 2) A nonlinear stochastic network simulation; 3) A real world 3D neuroscience dataset, applying interpretability analyses to verify the learning of accurate PEs. Overall, we find that a learned PE initialized from a small-norm distribution can 1) uncover interpretable PEs that mirror ground truth positions in multiple dimensions, and 2) lead to improved generalization. These results illustrate the feasibility of learning identifiable and interpretable PEs for enhanced generalization.

papers.title: Correlating Neural and Symbolic Representations of Language
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the correspondence between neural activation patterns and symbolic structures such as syntax trees? Do neural models encode syntactic information?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two RSA-based methods (Structured RSA and RSA_REGRESS) for correlating neural and symbolic representations, validates them on synthetic language, and applies them to show that neural models encode syntactic information, with syntax most salient in intermediate layers of BERT.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods are effective for correlating neural and symbolic representations and reveal that neural models encode syntactic information, with the highest encoding in intermediate layers.
papers.key_findings:
On synthetic language, the methods show the expected pattern: encoders trained on tasks requiring syntactic structure show higher correlation with tree kernel similarities.
Both Infersent and BERT encode syntactic information, with trained models showing higher correlation than random models.
In BERT, syntactic information peaks in intermediate layers (layers 15-22) and declines in later layers.
Randomly initialized models exhibit non-random activation patterns that correlate negatively with tree kernel similarities, indicating that learning must overcome initial biases.
RSA_REGRESS is less sensitive to the tree kernel discounting parameter λ than standard RSA.
future_direction: Apply the methods to other symbolic representations such as dependency trees or Abstract Meaning Representations.
papers.abstract: Analysis methods which enable us to better understand the representations and functioning of neural models of language are increasingly needed as deep learning becomes the dominant approach in NLP. Here we present two methods based on Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA) and Tree Kernels (TK) which allow us to directly quantify how strongly the information encoded in neural activation patterns corresponds to information represented by symbolic structures such as syntax trees. We first validate our methods on the case of a simple synthetic language for arithmetic expressions with clearly defined syntax and semantics, and show that they exhibit the expected pattern of results. We then apply our methods to correlate neural representations of English sentences with their constituency parse trees.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Towards Open-Ended Visual Scientific Discovery with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations.
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders can systematically recover semantic structure from foundation model representations without concept supervision, enabling open-ended feature discovery for scientific exploration.
papers.conclusion: SAEs provide a practical method for extracting interpretable features from vision foundation models, supporting open-ended discovery in scientific domains where target concepts are not pre-specified.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs outperform k-means and PCA on concept alignment metrics like mAP, Purity@k, and Coverage@τ.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve higher class coverage than standard SAEs on ADE20K.
SAEs can recover fine-grained anatomical parts from ecological images without labels.
Larger foundation models and later transformer layers lead to better concept rediscovery despite being harder to reconstruct.
Concept prevalence affects rediscovery; more common parts are recovered more reliably.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on ground-truth annotations to measure concept alignment, limiting assessment in truly unannotated domains.
Only visual examples are used to describe features; future work might use multimodal LLMs for language descriptions.
future_direction: Systematic evaluation of novel discoveries in unannotated domains.
Applying SAEs to non-vision foundation models.
papers.abstract: Scientific archives now contain hundreds of petabytes of data across genomics, ecology, climate, and molecular biology that could reveal undiscovered patterns if systematically analyzed at scale. Large-scale, weakly-supervised datasets in language and vision have driven the development of foundation models whose internal representations encode structure (patterns, co-occurrences and statistical regularities) beyond their training objectives. Most existing methods extract structure only for pre-specified targets; they excel at confirmation but do not support open-ended discovery of unknown patterns. We ask whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can enable open-ended feature discovery from foundation model representations. We evaluate this question in controlled rediscovery studies, where the learned SAE features are tested for alignment with semantic concepts on a standard segmentation benchmark and compared against strong label-free alternatives on concept-alignment metrics. Applied to ecological imagery, the same procedure surfaces fine-grained anatomical structure without access to segmentation or part labels, providing a scientific case study with ground-truth validation. While our experiments focus on vision with an ecology case study, the method is domain-agnostic and applicable to models in other sciences (e.g., proteins, genomics, weather). Our results indicate that sparse decomposition provides a practical instrument for exploring what scientific foundation models have learned, an important prerequisite for moving from confirmation to genuine discovery.

papers.title: Exploration and adaptation of large language models for specialized domains
papers.research_question: Can large language models overcome challenges in specialized domains, and how can they be effectively adapted to domain-specific requirements?
papers.core_contribution: The dissertation provides insights into the inner workings of LLMs and proposes adaptation methods that demonstrate LLMs can be effectively used in specialized domains, particularly clinical NLP.
papers.conclusion: The work provides new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models and multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.
papers.key_findings:
Layers of Transformer-based LLMs encode different dimensions of input text, with contextual representations and general language knowledge being beneficial for complex tasks.
Pre-trained language models outperform traditional approaches on clinical tasks.
Integration of domain-specific resources (like ICD hierarchy) improves model generalization.
Behavioral testing framework can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts.
Prototypical networks can provide interpretable diagnosis predictions.
papers.limitation: There is no ground truth in clinical data
future_direction: Integration of multimodal and multilingual data
Efficient methods for large language models
papers.abstract: Large language models have transformed the field of natural language processing (NLP). Their improved performance on various NLP benchmarks makes them a promising tool—also for the application in specialized domains. Such domains are characterized by highly trained professionals with particular domain expertise. Since these experts are rare, improving the efficiency of their work with automated systems is especially desirable. However, domain-specific text resources hold various challenges for NLP systems. These challenges include distinct language, noisy and scarce data, and a high level of variation. Further, specialized domains present an increased need for transparent systems since they are often applied in high stakes settings. In this dissertation, we examine whether large language models (LLMs) can overcome some of these challenges and propose methods to effectively adapt them to domain-specific requirements. We first investigate the inner workings and abilities of LLMs and show how they can fill the gaps that are present in previous NLP algorithms for specialized domains. To this end, we explore the sources of errors produced by earlier systems to identify which of them can be addressed by using LLMs. Following this, we take a closer look at how information is processed within Transformer-based LLMs to better understand their capabilities. We find that their layers encode different dimensions of the input text. Here, the contextual vector representation, and the general language knowledge learned during pre-training are especially beneficial for solving complex and multi-step tasks common in specialized domains. Following this exploration, we propose solutions for further adapting LLMs to the requirements of domain-specific tasks. We focus on the clinical domain, which incorporates many typical challenges found in specialized domains. We show how to improve generalization by integrating different domain-specific resources into our models. We further analyze the behavior of the produced models and propose a behavioral testing framework that can serve as a tool for communication with domain experts. Finally, we present an approach for incorporating the benefits of LLMs while fulfilling requirements such as interpretability and modularity. The presented solutions show improvements in performance on benchmark datasets and in manually conducted analyses with medical professionals. Our work provides both new insights into the inner workings of pre-trained language models as well as multiple adaptation methods showing that LLMs can be an effective tool for NLP in specialized domains.

papers.title: The Local Interaction Basis: Identifying Computationally-Relevant and Sparsely Interacting Features in Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Can the Local Interaction Basis (LIB) method find interpretable and sparsely-interacting features in neural networks, particularly in language models?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Local Interaction Basis (LIB), a method to transform neural network activations into a basis of computationally-relevant and sparsely-interacting features, and shows it works on toy models but not on language models.
papers.conclusion: LIB is promising on toy models but does not achieve interpretable and sparsely-interacting features on language models, likely due to the assumption of a linear non-overcomplete basis.
papers.key_findings:
LIB identifies more computationally-relevant features than PCA in modular addition and CIFAR-10 models.
LIB features interact more sparsely than PCA features in CIFAR-10 and some layers of language models.
LIB does not produce more interpretable features than PCA in language models.
Integrated gradient interaction graphs can aid circuit discovery in toy models.
LIB does not reveal modular structure in language models.
papers.limitation: LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models.
future_direction: Generalizing LIB to overcomplete bases to handle features in superposition.
Exploring other ways to average attributions over the dataset.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the behavior of neural networks by reverse-engineering their internal computations. However, current methods struggle to find clear interpretations of neural network activations because a decomposition of activations into computational features is missing. Individual neurons or model components do not cleanly correspond to distinct features or functions. We present a novel interpretability method that aims to overcome this limitation by transforming the activations of the network into a new basis - the Local Interaction Basis (LIB). LIB aims to identify computational features by removing irrelevant activations and interactions. Our method drops irrelevant activation directions and aligns the basis with the singular vectors of the Jacobian matrix between adjacent layers. It also scales features based on their importance for downstream computation, producing an interaction graph that shows all computationally-relevant features and interactions in a model. We evaluate the effectiveness of LIB on modular addition and CIFAR-10 models, finding that it identifies more computationally-relevant features that interact more sparsely, compared to principal component analysis. However, LIB does not yield substantial improvements in interpretability or interaction sparsity when applied to language models. We conclude that LIB is a promising theory-driven approach for analyzing neural networks, but in its current form is not applicable to large language models.

papers.title: Probing Graph Representations
papers.research_question: What is encoded in the representations learned by graph-based models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a probing framework to analyze graph representations and shows that transformer-based graph models capture more chemically relevant information compared to message-passing GNNs.
papers.conclusion: Probing is a useful diagnostic tool for understanding and evaluating graph-based models, especially in capturing domain-relevant information.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information in their representations.
Randomly initialized models can also encode useful features, sometimes on par with pretrained models.
Skip connections help preserve information across layers.
Pairwise probing can isolate the effect of specific properties and show causal relationships.
papers.abstract: Today we have a good theoretical understanding of the representational power of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). For example, their limitations have been characterized in relation to a hierarchy of Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) isomorphism tests. However, we do not know what is encoded in the learned representations. This is our main question. We answer it using a probing framework to quantify the amount of meaningful information captured in graph representations. Our findings on molecular datasets show the potential of probing for understanding the inductive biases of graph-based models. We compare different families of models and show that transformer-based models capture more chemically relevant information compared to models based on message passing. We also study the effect of different design choices such as skip connections and virtual nodes. We advocate for probing as a useful diagnostic tool for evaluating graph-based models.

papers.title: The geometry of BERT
papers.research_question: How does BERT's attention mechanism work internally, and what insights can be gained about its classification process?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel theoretical perspective on BERT's attention mechanism, introducing the concepts of directionality of subspace selection and cone index, and analyzes attention patterns and global information flow to understand its classification process.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides insights into BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models.
papers.key_findings:
The attention mechanism in BERT performs a subspace selection driven by the searching engine process (Q, K, V matrices).
The self-attention matrix exhibits specific, classifiable patterns (e.g., directional gate, open gate, contextual gates) that convey different types of information.
The cone index and distribution analysis show that lower layers specialize in finding information content, while upper layers primarily propagate it.
The information content propagates globally as a mean information content; the MLP synthesizes information from different heads, breaking the channel structure.
Rank collapse in attention is reinterpreted as a potential carrier of directional information rather than a purely negative phenomenon.
future_direction: Analysis of the BERT learning process during training.
Examining the specialization of individual components in the BERT architecture.
Leveraging these findings to optimize the architecture of the Transformer encoder.
papers.abstract: Transformer neural networks, particularly Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT), have shown remarkable performance across various tasks such as classification, text summarization, and question answering. However, their internal mechanisms remain mathematically obscure, highlighting the need for greater explainability and interpretability. In this direction, this paper investigates the internal mechanisms of BERT proposing a novel perspective on the attention mechanism of BERT from a theoretical perspective. The analysis encompasses both local and global network behavior. At the local level, the concept of directionality of subspace selection as well as a comprehensive study of the patterns emerging from the self-attention matrix are presented. Additionally, this work explores the semantic content of the information stream through data distribution analysis and global statistical measures including the novel concept of cone index. A case study on the classification of SARS-CoV-2 variants using RNA which resulted in a very high accuracy has been selected in order to observe these concepts in an application. The insights gained from this analysis contribute to a deeper understanding of BERT's classification process, offering potential avenues for future architectural improvements in Transformer models and further analysis in the training process.

papers.title: All Bark and No Bite: Rogue Dimensions in Transformer Language Models Obscure Representational Quality
papers.research_question: How informative are standard similarity measures (cosine similarity, Euclidean distance) in contextualized language models, and how do rogue dimensions dominate these measures, obscuring representational quality?
papers.core_contribution: Standard similarity measures in contextual language models are dominated by a small number of rogue dimensions, and simple postprocessing techniques like standardization can correct for this, revealing underlying representational quality that is preserved across all layers.
papers.conclusion: Standard similarity measures are not informative for contextual language models due to rogue dimensions, and accounting for these dimensions (e.g., via standardization) is essential for any similarity-based analysis.
papers.key_findings:
A small number of rogue dimensions (1-5) dominate cosine similarity and Euclidean distance in contextual language models.
Rogue dimensions are centered far from the origin and have disproportionately high variance.
The rogue dimensions that dominate similarity measures do not dominate model behavior; ablating them has little effect on the language modeling distribution.
Rogue dimensions are often correlated with specific tokens (e.g., punctuation) and positions (e.g., position zero).
After postprocessing (e.g., standardization), representational quality (correlation with human similarity judgments) improves and is preserved across all layers, contrary to previous claims of degradation in later layers.
future_direction: Designing and implementing language models that do not develop rogue dimensions in the first place.
Understanding how rogue dimensions arise over time during pretraining.
Using the MultiBERT checkpoints to study whether rogue dimensions are coincidental or requisite for good performance, and how they emerge.
papers.abstract: Similarity measures are a vital tool for understanding how language models represent and process language. Standard representational similarity measures such as cosine similarity and Euclidean distance have been successfully used in static word embedding models to understand how words cluster in semantic space. Recently, these measures have been applied to embeddings from contextualized models such as BERT and GPT-2. In this work, we call into question the informativity of such measures for contextualized language models. We find that a small number of rogue dimensions, often just 1-3, dominate these measures. Moreover, we find a striking mismatch between the dimensions that dominate similarity measures and those which are important to the behavior of the model. We show that simple postprocessing techniques such as standardization are able to correct for rogue dimensions and reveal underlying representational quality. We argue that accounting for rogue dimensions is essential for any similarity-based analysis of contextual language models.

papers.title: Mechanistic Permutability: Match Features Across Layers
papers.research_question: How do interpretable features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) evolve across layers in neural networks, and how can we align these features across layers without using input data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Match, a data-free method for aligning Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across neural network layers, and parameter folding, a technique that incorporates activation thresholds into SAE weights to account for feature scale differences and improve matching.
papers.conclusion: SAE Match advances mechanistic interpretability by providing a data-free tool for analyzing feature dynamics across layers, validated on Gemma 2, showing effective feature matching and persistence, and enabling approximation of hidden states.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Match effectively captures feature evolution across layers, improving feature matching quality.
Features persist over several layers, with similarity gradually declining but remaining significant for approximately five layers.
The method can approximate hidden states across layers, enabling layer pruning with minimal performance loss from the 10th layer onward.
Parameter folding, which incorporates activation thresholds into SAE weights, improves matching quality by accounting for differences in feature scales.
Matching quality is lower in initial layers (before layer 10), possibly due to more polysemantic features and differences in SAE sparsity (l0 norms).
papers.limitation:
The current work uses a scheme matching all SAE weights (encoder, decoder, biases); future studies may need a more precise understanding of the behavior of different weights within the module.
The method uses bijective matching, but some features are not matched in this way, suggesting a need for more sophisticated methods to understand feature dynamics.
Selecting appropriate SAEs based on their l0 value (sparsity) is important, as differences in l0 norms between layers can affect matching performance, especially in early layers.
future_direction: More precise understanding of the behavior of different SAE weights (encoder, decoder, biases) in matching.
Selecting SAEs based on their l0 value (sparsity) to improve matching, especially in early layers.
Exploring more sophisticated, non-bijective methods to understand feature dynamics when features are not perfectly matched.
papers.abstract: Understanding how features evolve across layers in deep neural networks is a fundamental challenge in mechanistic interpretability, particularly due to polysemanticity and feature superposition. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been used to extract interpretable features from individual layers, aligning these features across layers has remained an open problem. In this paper, we introduce SAE Match, a novel, data-free method for aligning SAE features across different layers of a neural network. Our approach involves matching features by minimizing the mean squared error between the folded parameters of SAEs, a technique that incorporates activation thresholds into the encoder and decoder weights to account for differences in feature scales. Through extensive experiments on the Gemma 2 language model, we demonstrate that our method effectively captures feature evolution across layers, improving feature matching quality. We also show that features persist over several layers and that our approach can approximate hidden states across layers. Our work advances the understanding of feature dynamics in neural networks and provides a new tool for mechanistic interpretability studies.

papers.title: The Locality and Symmetry of Positional Encodings
papers.research_question: What are the core properties of positional encodings in bidirectional masked language models, and how do they correlate with downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies locality and symmetry as fundamental properties of positional encodings in bidirectional masked language models, demonstrates their correlation with downstream task performance, and reveals a weakness of symmetry via new word-swap probing tasks.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that locality and symmetry are two key properties of positional encodings, with locality aiding local composition and symmetry having a flaw in handling semantic role swaps, and hopes these findings inspire better design of positional encodings.
papers.key_findings:
Positional encodings in BERT-style models exhibit locality and symmetry properties, which are learned during pre-training.
Higher locality and symmetry in positional encodings lead to better inductive bias and improved performance on downstream natural language understanding tasks.
Locality helps positional encodings capture short-distance syntactic dependencies, while contextual weights handle long-distance dependencies.
Symmetry, while beneficial for many tasks, causes models to be insensitive to semantic role swaps, as shown by new probing tasks (Constituency Shuffling and Semantic Role Shuffling).
Initializing positional encodings with suitable locality and symmetry properties improves model performance compared to random initialization.
papers.limitation:
Focus on bidirectional masked language models, not decoder-only models like GPT.
Analysis limited to English language; different languages have different word order properties.
Handcrafted positional encodings replicate limitations of current positional encodings and do not fully address the symmetry flaw.
future_direction: Study decoder-only language models (GPT-style) for positional encoding properties.
Extend analysis to other languages and include natural language generation tasks.
Develop architectures that address the symmetry flaw in positional encodings.
papers.abstract: Positional Encodings (PEs) are used to inject word-order information into transformer-based language models. While they can significantly enhance the quality of sentence representations, their specific contribution to language models is not fully understood, especially given recent findings that various positional encodings are insensitive to word order. In this work, we conduct a systematic study of positional encodings in \textbf{Bidirectional Masked Language Models} (BERT-style) , which complements existing work in three aspects: (1) We uncover the core function of PEs by identifying two common properties, Locality and Symmetry; (2) We show that the two properties are closely correlated with the performances of downstream tasks; (3) We quantify the weakness of current PEs by introducing two new probing tasks, on which current PEs perform poorly. We believe that these results are the basis for developing better PEs for transformer-based language models. The code is available at \faGithub~ \url{https://github.com/tigerchen52/locality\_symmetry}

papers.title: Probing Pretrained Language Models for Lexical Semantics
papers.research_question: How can lexical semantic knowledge be extracted from pretrained language models, how is this knowledge distributed across layers, and how do the extracted representations compare to traditional static word embeddings?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a systematic study of how to extract type-level lexical semantic knowledge from pretrained language models, showing that monolingual models store rich lexical information primarily in lower layers and that extracted vectors can outperform traditional word embeddings on several monolingual tasks.
papers.conclusion: Pretrained language models store a wealth of type-level lexical knowledge, and effectively uncovering this knowledge depends on careful configuration of extraction strategies, with universal best practices including using monolingual LMs, encoding words with multiple contexts, excluding special tokens, and averaging over lower layers.
papers.key_findings:
Lexical semantic knowledge is concentrated in the lower Transformer layers of pretrained language models.
Averaging representations across multiple layers yields better performance than using a single layer.
Monolingual language models contain more lexical information for a target language than massively multilingual models like mBERT.
Extracted 'BERT-based' static word embeddings outperform fastText on monolingual tasks (e.g., lexical similarity, analogy, relation prediction) but not on cross-lingual tasks (BLI, CLIR).
Translation pairs obtain similar representations in independently trained monolingual LMs, indicating approximate isomorphism between the monolingual spaces.
papers.limitation: The comparison with fastText word embeddings is not strictly apples-to-apples because the models were trained on different corpora (Wikipedia dumps for fastText vs. the corpora used for pretraining the LMs).
future_direction: Investigating how domains of external corpora affect the extraction of word representations and how to sample representative contexts.
Extending the study to more languages, more lexical semantic probes, and other larger underlying language models.
Developing more sophisticated lexical representation extraction methods, such as layer weighting or attention, and lightweight methods to enrich lexical content in multilingual LMs.
papers.abstract: The success of large pretrained language models (LMs) such as BERT and RoBERTa has sparked interest in probing their representations, in order to unveil what types of knowledge they implicitly capture. While prior research focused on morphosyntactic, semantic, and world knowledge, it remains unclear to which extent LMs also derive lexical type-level knowledge from words in context. In this work, we present a systematic empirical analysis across six typologically diverse languages and five different lexical tasks, addressing the following questions: 1) How do different lexical knowledge extraction strategies (monolingual versus multilingual source LM, out-ofcontext versus in-context encoding, inclusion of special tokens, and layer-wise averaging) impact performance? How consistent are the observed effects across tasks and languages? 2) Is lexical knowledge stored in few parameters, or is it scattered throughout the network? 3) How do these representations fare against traditional static word vectors in lexical tasks? 4) Does the lexical information emerging from independently trained monolingual LMs display latent similarities? Our main results indicate patterns and best practices that hold universally, but also point to prominent variations across languages and tasks. Moreover, we validate the claim that lower Transformer layers carry more type-level lexical knowledge, but also show that this knowledge is distributed across multiple layers.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models by resolving superposition, and can these features be used for causal analysis and circuit discovery?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoders provide a scalable, unsupervised method to find interpretable, monosemantic features in language models, enabling precise causal analysis and circuit discovery.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders are a scalable, unsupervised approach to disentangling language model features from superposition, facilitating interpretability, circuit mapping, and targeted model editing.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoder features are more interpretable than neurons, PCA, ICA, and random directions as measured by autointerpretability scores.
Sparse autoencoder features allow more precise localization of causally important features for the IOI task than PCA, requiring fewer patches to achieve a given KL divergence.
Individual features are monosemantic (e.g., an apostrophe feature) and have predictable effects on output logits, such as suppressing the 's' token after an apostrophe.
Sparse autoencoders enable automatic circuit detection across layers, as demonstrated for a closing parenthesis feature.
The method works well on residual stream activations but has limitations for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
papers.limitation:
The autoencoders do not achieve zero reconstruction loss, indicating they fail to capture all information in the activations.
Replacing activations with reconstructions increases perplexity, showing loss of information.
The method is less robust for MLP layers, where many features become dead.
Autointerpretability has limitations, such as GPT-4 struggling with patterns centered around next or previous tokens.
future_direction: Explore other sparse autoencoder architectures and minimize change in model outputs when replacing activations.
Incorporate information about model weights or dictionary features from adjacent layers into training.
Improve feature discovery in MLP and attention layers, and generalize to other tasks and behaviors.
papers.abstract: One of the roadblocks to a better understanding of neural networks' internals is \textit{polysemanticity}, where neurons appear to activate in multiple, semantically distinct contexts. Polysemanticity prevents us from identifying concise, human-understandable explanations for what neural networks are doing internally. One hypothesised cause of polysemanticity is \textit{superposition}, where neural networks represent more features than they have neurons by assigning features to an overcomplete set of directions in activation space, rather than to individual neurons. Here, we attempt to identify those directions, using sparse autoencoders to reconstruct the internal activations of a language model. These autoencoders learn sets of sparsely activating features that are more interpretable and monosemantic than directions identified by alternative approaches, where interpretability is measured by automated methods. Moreover, we show that with our learned set of features, we can pinpoint the features that are causally responsible for counterfactual behaviour on the indirect object identification task \citep{wang2022interpretability} to a finer degree than previous decompositions. This work indicates that it is possible to resolve superposition in language models using a scalable, unsupervised method. Our method may serve as a foundation for future mechanistic interpretability work, which we hope will enable greater model transparency and steerability.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Fine-tuning and Sentence-level Probing for Linguistic Knowledge in Pre-trained Transformers
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the representations and linguistic knowledge in pre-trained transformer models, and to what extent can changes in probing accuracy be attributed to changes in linguistic knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that fine-tuning pre-trained transformer models affects sentence-level probing accuracy, but these changes are not straightforward and often not due to acquisition or loss of linguistic knowledge; instead, they can be attributed to changes in attention distribution or other factors, requiring careful interpretation.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that fine-tuning can lead to substantial changes in probing accuracy, but these changes require careful interpretation as they may not directly indicate changes in linguistic knowledge.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning affects probing accuracy, with changes typically larger for higher layers.
Changes in probing accuracy vary across models, fine-tuning tasks, and probing tasks.
Improvements in probing accuracy with CLS-pooling can be attributed to changes in attention distribution rather than acquisition of new linguistic knowledge.
Fine-tuning can negatively affect probing accuracy, possibly due to changes in representations.
Only in few cases does fine-tuning improve probing accuracy beyond using a strong pooling method like mean-pooling.
papers.limitation: It remains unclear whether fine-tuning indeed removes the linguistic knowledge or whether it is simply no longer linearly separable.
future_direction: Further investigation into whether fine-tuning removes linguistic knowledge or just makes it not linearly separable.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning pre-trained contextualized embedding models has become an integral part of the NLP pipeline. At the same time, probing has emerged as a way to investigate the linguistic knowledge captured by pre-trained models. Very little is, however, understood about how fine-tuning affects the representations of pre-trained models and thereby the linguistic knowledge they encode. This paper contributes towards closing this gap. We study three different pre-trained models: BERT, RoBERTa, and ALBERT, and investigate through sentence-level probing how finetuning affects their representations. We find that for some probing tasks fine-tuning leads to substantial changes in accuracy, possibly suggesting that fine-tuning introduces or even removes linguistic knowledge from a pre-trained model. These changes, however, vary greatly across different models, fine-tuning and probing tasks. Our analysis reveals that while finetuning indeed changes the representations of a pre-trained model and these changes are typically larger for higher layers, only in very few cases, fine-tuning has a positive effect on probing accuracy that is larger than just using the pre-trained model with a strong pooling method. Based on our findings, we argue that both positive and negative effects of finetuning on probing require a careful interpretation.

papers.title: Syntactic Perturbations Reveal Representational Correlates of Hierarchical Phrase Structure in Pretrained Language Models
papers.research_question: What aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by pretrained language model representations, and how are they built along the layers of the network?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that input perturbations reveal how transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and that such perturbations are a useful analysis tool for interpreting deep language models.
papers.conclusion: Transformers build sensitivity to hierarchical phrase structure across layers, and attention changes partially explain this sensitivity.
papers.key_findings:
Representations are more distorted by shuffling small n-grams in early layers and by large n-grams in later layers, indicating increasing context scale along layers.
Swapping phrases causes less distortion than swapping non-phrases, indicating sensitivity to phrase structure.
Swapping adjacent words across phrase boundaries causes more distortion than within boundaries, and distortion increases with syntactic distance, especially in deeper layers.
Attention changes partially explain the sensitivity to syntactic distance.
The distortion metric correlates with impairment of syntactic probes (POS, grandparent tags, tree distance).
future_direction: Developing a formal theory of efficient hierarchical data representations in distributed features.
Searching for causal connection between attention structure, representational geometry, and model performance.
Applying perturbation analyses to models trained on shuffled data or models with explicit syntax.
papers.abstract: While vector-based language representations from pretrained language models have set a new standard for many NLP tasks, there is not yet a complete accounting of their inner workings. In particular, it is not entirely clear what aspects of sentence-level syntax are captured by these representations, nor how (if at all) they are built along the stacked layers of the network.
